title: Chemical Kinetics (Rate Law, Order, Molecularity, & Integrated Rate Equations)
syllabus: Rate of a chemical reaction (average and instantaneous rate); Factors affecting the rate of reaction: concentration, temperature, pressure, and catalyst; Rate law expression and specific rate constant (k); Order and molecularity of elementary and complex reactions; Units of rate constant for nth order reactions; Integrated rate laws and half-life expressions for zero-order and first-order reactions; Graphical representations of zero and first-order kinetics; Pseudo-first-order reactions (inversion of cane sugar, hydrolysis of esters); Methods for determining reaction order (initial rates method, integrated rate method, half-life method)

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] For a chemical reaction $A + 2B \rightarrow C$, the rate equation is experimentally found to be $\text{Rate} = k[A]^1 [B]^2$. If the volume of the reaction vessel is suddenly reduced to one-third of its initial volume at constant temperature, the rate of the reaction will become:
questions.solution:
Let initial concentrations of $A$ and $B$ be $[A]_0$ and $[B]_0$.
Initial rate:
$$r_1 = k[A]_0 [B]_0^2$$
When the volume of the container is decreased to $\frac{1}{3}$ of its original volume ($V_2 = \frac{V_1}{3}$), the concentration of each gaseous or solution species triples:
$$[A]' = 3[A]_0, \quad [B]' = 3[B]_0$$
New reaction rate:
$$r_2 = k[A]' [B]'^2 = k(3[A]_0)(3[B]_0)^2 = k(3[A]_0)(9[B]_0^2) = 27 \cdot k[A]_0 [B]_0^2 = 27 r_1$$
Therefore, the rate of the reaction increases by a factor of $27$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] A first-order reaction is $50\%$ complete in $20\text{ minutes}$ at $300\text{ K}$. The time required for $99.9\%$ completion of the same reaction is approximately:
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction:
$$t_{1/2} = 20\text{ min}$$
Rate constant:
$$k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{20\text{ min}}$$
For $99.9\%$ completion:
$$[A]_t = [A]_0 - 0.999[A]_0 = 0.001[A]_0 = 10^{-3}[A]_0$$
Using the integrated first-order rate law:
$$t_{99.9\%} = \frac{2.303}{k} \log_{10}\left(\frac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}\right) = \frac{2.303}{k} \log_{10}\left(\frac{[A]_0}{10^{-3}[A]_0}\right) = \frac{2.303}{k} \log_{10}(10^3) = \frac{2.303 \times 3}{k} = \frac{6.909}{k}$$
Since $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$:
$$t_{99.9\%} = \frac{6.909}{0.693} \times t_{1/2} \approx 10 \times t_{1/2}$$
$$t_{99.9\%} = 10 \times 20\text{ min} = 200\text{ minutes}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] For the reaction $2A + B \rightarrow 3C + D$, which of the following expressions correctly represents the rate of reaction?
questions.solution:
The rate of a chemical reaction is defined by the rate of disappearance of reactants (with a negative sign) or the rate of appearance of products (with a positive sign), divided by their respective stoichiometric coefficients:
$$\text{Rate} = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[A]}{dt} = -\frac{1}{1}\frac{d[B]}{dt} = +\frac{1}{3}\frac{d[C]}{dt} = +\frac{1}{1}\frac{d[D]}{dt}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] The rate constant of a chemical reaction has the units $\text{L}^2\text{ mol}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$. The overall order of this reaction is:
questions.solution:
The general formula for the units of a rate constant $k$ for an $n^{\text{th}}$-order reaction is:
$$\text{Units of } k = (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1 - n} \text{ s}^{-1} = \text{mol}^{1-n} \text{ L}^{n-1} \text{ s}^{-1}$$
Given units: $\text{L}^2\text{ mol}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$:
Comparing the exponent of $\text{L}$:
$$n - 1 = 2 \implies n = 3$$
Or comparing the exponent of $\text{mol}$:
$$1 - n = -2 \implies n = 3$$
Thus, the reaction is of the third order ($n = 3$).

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] A plot of $[A]$ versus time $t$ for the reaction $A \rightarrow \text{Products}$ yields a straight line with a negative slope equal to $-0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$ and y-intercept equal to $0.5\text{ mol L}^{-1}$. The order of the reaction and the time required for complete consumption of $A$ are:
questions.solution:
1. The integrated rate equation for a zero-order reaction is:
$$[A]_t = -k t + [A]_0$$
Comparing with $y = mx + c$, a plot of $[A]$ versus $t$ gives a straight line with slope $m = -k$ and intercept $c = [A]_0$.
Since the plot of $[A]$ versus $t$ is linear, the reaction is strictly zero-order.
2. Given:
- Slope $=-k = -0.02 \implies k = 0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$
- Intercept $=[A]_0 = 0.5\text{ mol L}^{-1}$
3. Time for complete reaction ($[A]_t = 0$):
$$t_{\text{complete}} = \frac{[A]_0}{k} = \frac{0.5\text{ mol L}^{-1}}{0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}} = 25\text{ seconds}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] For an elementary reaction $2X + Y \rightarrow Z$, the molecularity and order of the reaction are respectively:
questions.solution:
1. For an elementary reaction (a single-step reaction occurring in one collision), the molecularity is the total number of reactant molecules colliding simultaneously, which is $2 + 1 = 3$ (termolecular).
2. For any elementary reaction, the order with respect to each reactant is equal to its stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced equation:
$$\text{Rate} = k[X]^2 [Y]^1$$
$$\text{Overall order} = 2 + 1 = 3$$
Hence, both molecularity and order are equal to $3$.

questions.question:
[JEE Main 2021] Hydrolysis of ethyl acetate in the presence of excess aqueous mineral acid:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$$
This reaction is an example of a:
questions.solution:
In acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis, the true theoretical rate law is second order:
$$\text{Rate} = k'[\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5][\text{H}_2\text{O}]$$
However, water is present in enormous excess ($[\text{H}_2\text{O}] \approx 55.5\text{ M}$) compared to the ester ($0.01 - 0.1\text{ M}$), so its concentration remains practically constant throughout the course of the reaction.
Combining constants: $k = k'[\text{H}_2\text{O}]$, the rate law simplifies to:
$$\text{Rate} = k[\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5]$$
A second-order reaction that behaves kinetically as a first-order reaction due to the large excess of one reactant is classified as a pseudo-first-order reaction.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] For a reaction $A \rightarrow B$, the half-life period ($t_{1/2}$) is doubled when the initial concentration of $A$ is doubled. The order of this reaction is:
questions.solution:
The general relation between half-life ($t_{1/2}$) and initial concentration ($[A]_0$) for an $n^{\text{th}}$-order reaction is:
$$t_{1/2} \propto \frac{1}{[A]_0^{n - 1}} = [A]_0^{1 - n}$$
Given that when $[A]_0$ is doubled, $t_{1/2}$ also doubles ($t_{1/2} \propto [A]_0^1$):
$$1 - n = 1 \implies n = 0$$
Therefore, the reaction is of zero order ($t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k}$).

questions.question:
[JEE Main 2020] The following initial rate data were obtained for the reaction $2A + B \rightarrow C$:

| Experiment | $[A]$ (M) | $[B]$ (M) | Initial Rate ($\text{M s}^{-1}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $0.10$ | $0.10$ | $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 2 | $0.20$ | $0.10$ | $4.0 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 3 | $0.20$ | $0.20$ | $1.6 \times 10^{-2}$ |

The rate law for the reaction is:
questions.solution:
Let the rate law be $\text{Rate} = k[A]^x [B]^y$.
1. Compare Experiments 1 and 2 (where $[B]$ is constant at $0.10\text{ M}$):
$$\frac{\text{Rate}_2}{\text{Rate}_1} = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \left(\frac{0.20}{0.10}\right)^x$$
$$2 = 2^x \implies x = 1$$
2. Compare Experiments 2 and 3 (where $[A]$ is constant at $0.20\text{ M}$):
$$\frac{\text{Rate}_3}{\text{Rate}_2} = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-2}}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{16 \times 10^{-3}}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \left(\frac{0.20}{0.10}\right)^y$$
$$4 = 2^y \implies 2^2 = 2^y \implies y = 2$$
Therefore, the rate law is $\text{Rate} = k[A][B]^2$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] Which of the following statements regarding the molecularity of a reaction is INCORRECT?
options: Molecularity can be zero, fractional, or negative
Molecularity is defined only for elementary reactions
Molecularity is the number of reacting species colliding simultaneously in a single elementary step
Molecularity rarely exceeds three due to the low probability of more than three molecules colliding simultaneously
questions.solution:
1. Molecularity is an integer count of real colliding particles taking part in an elementary chemical step; hence, it can only be a positive whole number ($1, 2, 3$). It can never be zero, fractional, or negative.
2. In contrast, reaction order is an experimentally determined quantity that can be zero, fractional, positive, or negative.
Therefore, Statement A is incorrect.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] For a first-order gas-phase reaction $A(g) \rightarrow B(g) + C(g)$, the initial pressure is $P_0$ and the total pressure at time $t$ is $P_t$. The integrated rate equation for the rate constant $k$ is:
questions.solution:
Let the decrease in partial pressure of $A(g)$ at time $t$ be $p$:
- Initially ($t = 0$): $P_A = P_0, \quad P_B = 0, \quad P_C = 0$
- At time $t$: $P_A = P_0 - p, \quad P_B = p, \quad P_C = p$
Total pressure at time $t$:
$$P_t = P_A + P_B + P_C = (P_0 - p) + p + p = P_0 + p$$
$$p = P_t - P_0$$
Partial pressure of reactant $A$ at time $t$:
$$P_A = P_0 - p = P_0 - (P_t - P_0) = 2P_0 - P_t$$
Substitute into the integrated first-order rate law:
$$k = \frac{2.303}{t} \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_{A,0}}{P_{A,t}}\right) = \frac{2.303}{t} \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_0}{2P_0 - P_t}\right)$$

questions.question: For a second-order reaction $A \rightarrow \text{Products}$, which of the following plots will be linear?
questions.solution:
The integrated rate equation for a second-order reaction $-\frac{d[A]}{dt} = k[A]^2$ is:
$$\frac{1}{[A]_t} - \frac{1}{[A]_0} = k t \implies \frac{1}{[A]_t} = k t + \frac{1}{[A]_0}$$
Comparing with $y = mx + c$:
- $y = \frac{1}{[A]_t}$
- $x = t$
- $\text{Slope } m = +k$
- $\text{Intercept } c = \frac{1}{[A]_0}$
Thus, the plot of $\frac{1}{[A]}$ versus $t$ is a straight line with a positive slope.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] A radioactive isotope decays with a half-life of $14\text{ days}$. Starting with $100\text{ g}$ of the pure isotope, the mass remaining undecayed after $56\text{ days}$ is:
questions.solution:
All radioactive decay processes follow first-order kinetics.
Number of half-lives elapsed ($n$):
$$n = \frac{t}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{56\text{ days}}{14\text{ days}} = 4$$
The amount remaining after $n$ half-lives is:
$$N = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n = 100\text{ g} \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4 = 100 \times \frac{1}{16} = 6.25\text{ g}$$

questions.question:
[JEE Main 2020] In a reaction between $A$ and $B$, the initial rate of reaction was measured for various concentrations as shown:

If $[A]$ is kept constant and $[B]$ is tripled, the rate increases by a factor of $9$.
If both $[A]$ and $[B]$ are doubled, the rate increases by a factor of $8$.

The order of reaction with respect to $A$ and $B$ respectively are:
questions.solution:
Let the rate equation be $r = k[A]^x [B]^y$.
1. When $[B]$ is tripled and $[A]$ is kept constant:
$$\frac{r'}{r} = 3^y = 9 = 3^2 \implies y = 2$$
2. When both $[A]$ and $[B]$ are doubled:
$$\frac{r''}{r} = 2^x \cdot 2^y = 8 = 2^3$$
$$2^{x + y} = 2^3 \implies x + y = 3$$
Substitute $y = 2$:
$$x + 2 = 3 \implies x = 1$$
Thus, the order with respect to $A$ is $1$ and with respect to $B$ is $2$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] For a zero-order reaction $A \rightarrow B$, if the initial concentration is $0.2\text{ M}$ and the rate constant is $0.002\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$, the concentration of $A$ remaining after $40\text{ seconds}$ is:
questions.solution:
Using the integrated rate equation for a zero-order reaction:
$$[A]_t = [A]_0 - k t$$
Substitute $[A]_0 = 0.2\text{ M}$, $k = 0.002\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$, and $t = 40\text{ s}$:
$$[A]_t = 0.2 - (0.002 \times 40) = 0.2 - 0.08 = 0.12\text{ M}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] For a first-order reaction $A \rightarrow \text{Products}$, the ratio of the time required for $75\%$ completion ($t_{75\%}$) to the time required for $50\%$ completion ($t_{50\%}$) is:
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction:
1. At $50\%$ completion, half of the reactant has reacted: $[A]_t = \frac{[A]_0}{2}$, so $t_{50\%} = t_{1/2}$.
2. At $75\%$ completion, $\frac{3}{4}$ of the reactant has reacted, leaving $\frac{1}{4}$ of the initial amount: $[A]_t = \frac{[A]_0}{4} = \frac{[A]_0}{2^2}$.
Because remaining concentration reduces by half every $t_{1/2}$, reaching $\frac{1}{4}$ requires exactly two half-lives:
$$t_{75\%} = 2 \times t_{50\%}$$
$$\frac{t_{75\%}}{t_{50\%}} = 2$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] The rate of a gaseous reaction is expressed as $\text{Rate} = k[NO]^2 [O_2]$. If the pressure of the reaction mixture is doubled by reducing the volume at constant temperature, the rate of reaction will:
questions.solution:
By the ideal gas law, $P = CRT \implies C \propto P$.
Doubling the total pressure doubles the partial pressure and molar concentration of each component:
$$[NO]' = 2[NO], \quad [O_2]' = 2[O_2]$$
New rate:
$$r' = k(2[NO])^2 (2[O_2]) = k(4[NO]^2)(2[O_2]) = 8 \cdot k[NO]^2 [O_2] = 8r$$
Thus, the rate increases by a factor of $8$.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding a zero-order reaction?
options: The rate of reaction is independent of the reactant concentration
The half-life of the reaction is independent of initial concentration
A plot of $\ln[A]$ versus $t$ is linear
The rate constant has the unit $\text{s}^{-1}$
questions.solution:
For a zero-order reaction:
$$\text{Rate} = k[A]^0 = k$$
1. The rate is constant and completely independent of the concentration of the reactants.
2. Half-life depends directly on the initial concentration: $t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k}$.
3. The linear plot is $[A]$ versus $t$, not $\ln[A]$ versus $t$.
4. The unit of $k$ is $\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] In the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, $2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{O}_2(g)$, the rate of formation of $\text{O}_2$ is $0.016\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ min}^{-1}$. The rate of disappearance of $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ is:
questions.solution:
Equating the stoichiometric rates of the reaction:
$$\text{Rate} = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]}{dt} = +\frac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt}$$
$$\text{Rate of disappearance of } \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 = -\frac{d[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]}{dt} = 2 \times \frac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt}$$
Substitute $\frac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt} = 0.016\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ min}^{-1}$:
$$-\frac{d[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]}{dt} = 2 \times 0.016 = 0.032\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ min}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
[JEE Main 2020] Inversion of cane sugar (sucrose) in an acidic aqueous solution:
$$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\text{ (glucose)} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\text{ (fructose)}$$
Is monitored using a polarimeter. The rate constant $k$ in terms of optical rotations $r_0$ (initial), $r_t$ (at time $t$), and $r_\infty$ (at infinite time) is given by:
questions.solution:
Let the optical rotation be proportional to concentration:
1. At $t = 0$: $a \propto (r_0 - r_\infty)$ (where $a$ is initial sucrose concentration)
2. At time $t$: $(a - x) \propto (r_t - r_\infty)$ (where $a - x$ is remaining sucrose concentration)
Substitute into the first-order rate formula:
$$k = \frac{2.303}{t} \log_{10}\left(\frac{a}{a - x}\right) = \frac{2.303}{t} \log_{10}\left(\frac{r_0 - r_\infty}{r_t - r_\infty}\right)$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] A first-order reaction has a rate constant $k = 2.303 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$. Find the time (in seconds) required for the reactant concentration to fall to $\frac{1}{10}$ of its initial value.
questions.solution:
Using the integrated first-order rate law:
$$t = \frac{2.303}{k} \log_{10}\left(\frac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}\right)$$
Here $\frac{[A]_0}{[A]_t} = 10$:
$$t = \frac{2.303}{2.303 \times 10^{-3}} \log_{10}(10) = \frac{1}{10^{-3}} \times 1 = 1000.0\text{ seconds}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] For a zero-order reaction, the half-life period is $100\text{ minutes}$ when the initial concentration is $0.4\text{ M}$. Calculate the rate constant $k$ (in $\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{ min}^{-1}$, express as decimal).
questions.solution:
For a zero-order reaction:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k}$$
$$k = \frac{[A]_0}{2 \cdot t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.4\text{ mol L}^{-1}}{2 \times 100\text{ min}} = \frac{0.4}{200} = 0.002\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ min}^{-1}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] A first-order reaction is $75\%$ completed in $32\text{ minutes}$. Calculate the half-life period $t_{1/2}$ (in minutes) of the reaction.
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction:
$$t_{75\%} = 2 \times t_{1/2}$$
$$32 = 2 \times t_{1/2} \implies t_{1/2} = \frac{32}{2} = 16.0\text{ minutes}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] For a reaction $A \rightarrow B$, the rate law is $\text{Rate} = k[A]^{1/2}$. What is the overall order of the reaction (as a decimal)?
questions.solution:
The order of a reaction is defined as the sum of exponents of concentration terms in the rate law expression.
Here, the exponent of $[A]$ is $\frac{1}{2}$.
$$\text{Order} = 0.5$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] In a reaction $2A \rightarrow \text{Products}$, the concentration of $A$ decreases from $0.5\text{ mol L}^{-1}$ to $0.4\text{ mol L}^{-1}$ in $10\text{ minutes}$. Find the rate of disappearance of $A$ during this interval (in $\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{ min}^{-1}$).
questions.solution:
Rate of disappearance of $A$:
$$-\frac{\Delta[A]}{\Delta t} = -\frac{[A]_2 - [A]_1}{t_2 - t_1} = -\frac{0.4 - 0.5}{10} = -\frac{-0.1}{10} = 0.01\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ min}^{-1}$$
